rules_text:
Rules summary Contents 1 Game play 1.1 Assign reporters 1.2 Reassign a reporter 1.3 Recall reporters 1.4 Go to press 2 Game end 3 Scoring 3.1 Tiebreaker Game play On your turn, do one of four things: Assign reporters Select the arrow next to a story. Select how many meeples (reporters) to move from your player mat onto that story. Reassign a reporter Select a meeple on the board. Select another story. Recall reporters Select any number of meeples on the board to return to your player mat. Go to press You must pick up the stories where you have the majority of meeples (shared majority counts) and lay out a newspaper page with them. You can rotate stories to make them fit. Make sure you can fit in the available free spaces, and around the advertisement. All top stories (highest News Beat Value ) have to be placed first. As many top stories as possible have to touch the top of the page. Game end Triggered when a player publishes their third (4-5 players) or fourth (3 players) newspaper. Each other player has one last turn, but they can only move one meeple on that turn. Then each other player gets a mandatory publishing turn. Scoring For each paper you publish, you score: • The News Beat Value for every story on your page. (See the arrow on the board!) • The negative values on your page that are visible. • Double News Beat Value for one non-top story that touches the top of the page (your exclusive). • You lose News Beat Value in points for every story that doesn't fit. • You never score less than zero for a front page. Other ways to score points are: • If someone publishes a story that you have meeples on, you score the lower value of that News Beat (scoop points). • At the end of the game, whoever has the most stars of one News Beat gets the bonus points (see the track on top of the board) for that News Beat. All ties are awarded the full amount. Tiebreaker In the event of a tie for overall score, the player with the most stories wins. If still tied, the game is a tie with no winner. (The official rules add "If you really, really don’t like ties, flip a penny to determine the winner.", but BGA does not include this as an option.)

[Rating: 3/10] A very surprising flop. This game had me quite excited, but that quickly evaporated after playing. The ideas at play are neat, but the gameplay was dreadful. I was convinced I had been taught the game incorrectly, but after reading the rulebook myself, I realized that this game just wasn't fun. The game feels much more like a race than a strategic area control game, and this limits my enjoyment of it greatly. Considering its triumph of Tabletop Deathmatch, this dislike was all the more surprising. But, the box art is one of my favorites.

[Rating: 3/10] Whilst I liked the theme of this game, the mechanics just didn't seem to fit right for me, it seems like a good idea that was poorly executed.

[Rating: 3/10] This game is aggravating because there are a few good ideas here, just very poorly thrown together. They are about a year of development away from something worthwhile. Also the rulebook just doesn’t explain a key mechanism of the game, it only accidentally mentions it in an example. This was wild to me. A whole part of the game was just glossed over.

[Rating: 4/10] FOR TRADE ONLY KS Edition Absolutely horrible as a 2 player game (my main count for games).  I hate games that treat 2-player as an after thought and make up "alternate rules" for that count.  Only marginally better with more players.  Disappointed because it looks so promising on paper, but I can't even get it to the table in my groups anymore. Yet another KS game that promises big things, but fails to deliver on the important element of game play.

Despite this being primarily a race game, you are competing for points, and there are rewards when someone snatches a tile out from under your meeple.
